transcript.answer: Otto uses one server-side key because the delivered OLT TMS API only supports that. It authenticates every request with a single global `x-api-key` header. It has no user login, no login endpoint, no OAuth flow and no per-user credential. The kick-off options were Option A (each user forwards their own TMS credential) and Option B (re:cinq exchanges or holds per-user credentials). Option A was rejected because a user can't present a credential that doesn't exist. Option B fails because re:cinq can't exchange or hold one either. Option C is a server-held key with the customer boundary enforced in Otto's own code. It is the only option the API supports, and ADR-001 accepts it. The TMS key is company-scoped, so it can't narrow results by user or role. Otto therefore enforces the 'customers only see their own bookings' requirement itself. Clerk authenticates the user, and the Clerk organisation maps to the TMS `customerNumber`. A scope resolver (`apps/api/src/tools/toolAuth.ts`) derives that `customerNumber` from the authenticated company, never from the model or the request. Every TMS tool call goes through that resolver.

judgements.reason: The answer correctly says the TMS has no user-level auth, so forwarding is impossible, and that Otto enforces the customer boundary itself with one global key, but it omits that per-user credentials are moot because the TMS issues one key per integration partner.
